en: Preface to the Commentary on the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*.
This commentary was transcribed on the twenty-seventh day of the sixth month in the fourth year of the Daye era, following a single session of oral exposition.

The principles of this preface are profound and its subject matter vast; its language is concise yet its meaning is comprehensive. One must first gain a rough understanding of these six sections before one can proceed to read it.
First, one must have a profound understanding of the intent of the *Abhidharmakośa*;
second, one must be thoroughly versed in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;
third, one must skillfully comprehend the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Fourth, he was adept at examining the works of Laozi and Zhuangzi;
fifth, he extensively sought out the Confucian classics;
sixth, he was skilled in composing literary works.
In the past, I have already composed the "Profound and Correct Words" (Xuanzhengyan) preface to the *Sanlun* treatises.
This was written by that person (Senglang), and I did not provide a commentary on it myself;
however, whenever my teacher lectured, he would invariably read this preface.
However, as those of shallow understanding often harbor many confused and erroneous views, I have briefly set forth the essential framework to bestow upon my disciples.
The preface is divided into six sections;
the first delineates the Great宗 (Principle).
First, the explanation of the title;
second, the statement of the purpose for composing the treatise;
third, the praise of the treatise’s efficacy.
Five, the benefits of the treatise;
six, the author’s modesty.
Regarding the Middle Way of the True Nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), Part One: Establishing the Great Thesis.
"To find the mean" (zhèzhōng) means to break things so that they are level;
this is called "finding the mean.
As the Book says:
A single phrase can break jade; this treatise clarifies that the principles of birth-and-death, nirvana, and the myriad transformations are themselves the true mark (dharmatā).
Therefore, it is said: "The true mark is the breaking point."
There are two general intentions for making these remarks:
first, to praise this treatise;
second, to censure others.
There were four other individuals in total,
all of whom were proficient in the ultimate reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa), yet they were all refuted and found wanting.
The first was the way of the mundane world (laukikamārga).
All these are methods for securing one's household and state that are impure;
they do not accord with the central truth of the true nature (*dharmatā*).
Second, there are the ninety-six arts.
Wishing to clarify that one's own path is the truth,
[the opponent] claims that all else is merely false and not the true nature;
thus, their refutation misses the mark.
Third, there were five hundred masters of the Hīnayāna śāstras,
each adhering to the view that the characteristics of all phenomena possess determinate marks and thus failing to believe in the dharma of ultimate emptiness;
they also sought to clarify the true mark [of reality] without striking the middle way.
Fourth is the case of those Mahāyāna practitioners who grasp at attainments;
though they believe in ultimate emptiness, their dull faculties bring about their own ruin,
like one unskilled in incantations or one who improperly handles a venomous snake.
They are harmed by the view of emptiness;
they are like those who strike and miss the mark.
Therefore, he singles out and rebukes other people.
Now, [the master] Jingcheng praises this treatise by Nāgārjuna as elucidating the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and being the "middle way.
Therefore, it is called the middle way of the true mark.
Question: What is the true mark?
The answer to Master Rui’s later explanation consists of ten points of "not":
namely, not internal,
not external, and so forth.
Not a person,
not a dharma,
and not a condition.
It is not contemplation;
it is neither real nor unreal;
it is not attainment.
It is not lost;
therefore, it is called the true mark (lakṣaṇa).
This is the essential method of the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
The true mark refers to the object of contemplation;
the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) refers to the wisdom that illuminates it.
Without the true mark, there would be no basis for generating true contemplation.
Without the contemplation of non-reality, there is no means to illuminate the true mark of reality (*dharmatā*).
Although object and wisdom appear distinct, in truth both the object of cognition and the contemplation are quiescent.
These two phrases encompass every principle and include every word.
Although the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra* and the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* differ in their titles and sections,
they are largely identical in their meaning regarding the refutation of errors and the revelation of the Way;
the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is precisely the Middle Way.
The "site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa) refers to correct contemplation.
To proclaim this through the mouth is called "discourse" (lun).
Furthermore, the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is itself the Prajñāpāramitā of the true mark.
The illumination of the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) refers to contemplative prajñā (pratyavekṣaṇā-prajñā).
To proclaim these two meanings is called the prajñā of words (vyañjana-prajñā).
Furthermore, the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is the Buddha-nature as the objective realm (viṣaya).
The "site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa) refers to the nature of contemplative wisdom and the fruit of bodhi.
When contemplation is clear, all afflictions are pacified;
this is the nature of the fruit of fruits.
To speak of these four [aspects] is to open up that which is neither an object, nor contemplation, nor wisdom, nor cessation; this is precisely the Middle Way and true nature.
Therefore, one sees the Buddha-nature while sitting at the site of enlightenment and only then attains Buddhahood.
One should provide this explanation.
Question: Why is it called the "Manual of Essential Procedures" (*yāoga*) when it clarifies the *maṇḍala*?
Answer: The *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, in its "Chapter on Dharma," states:
There are three types of those who attain the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa),
namely, the persons of the Three Vehicles.
As the Nirvāṇa-sūtra says:
There are four grades of those who perceive the Middle Way:
because they observe with inferior wisdom, they attain the enlightenment of a śrāvaka;
up to, because they observe with the highest-of-the-high wisdom, they attain the enlightenment of all Buddhas.
Now, I wish to distinguish these from the two vehicles.
The followers of the two vehicles have not yet fathomed the source of the true mark (dharmatā),
whereas the Great Beings (mahāsattva) are precisely those who exhaust its principle.
Therefore, it is specifically called the "Path of the Dharma-Assembly.
As for its essential guidelines, they clarify the guidelines of the true nature (*dharmatā*).
There are three treatises in total.
First, the extensiveness of the *Vigrahavyāvartanī*;
second, the middle way of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*;
third, the summary of this present treatise.
Although the words here are concise, they constitute the essential means for entering the path of practice.
While various Mahāyāna treatises exist that are so extensive as to be difficult to investigate,
this treatise is brief in expression yet profound in its penetration of the truth.
Therefore, it is called "essential.
Furthermore, because Master Rui clearly realized the true mark (dharmatā), all beings obtained two benefits:
first, those in the six realms turned back from their former ways, and those of the three vehicles changed their course.
This means that all accumulated defilements are exhausted without exception.
Next, having completed the orderly return of the carriage to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), one directs the mind toward the stage of Buddhahood.
This refers precisely to the fact that all virtues are perfected without exception.
Furthermore, the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is a synonym for suchness (tathatā),
meaning the object of suchness;
the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is the wisdom of suchness.
These two are precisely the two dharma-bodies;
proclaiming these two types is called the "Responsive Transformation" (nirmāṇakāya).
This is the "Chapter on Manifesting the Golden Light of the Three Bodies."
In the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the true nature (*dharmatā*) is the Dharmakāya;
the illumination at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) is called the internal Nirmāṇakāya;
and the teaching of these two meanings is called the external Nirmāṇakāya.
Furthermore, the true mark (dharmatā) is precisely the primordially existent nirvāṇa,
while the illumination of the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is the sense of that which exists through beginning.
Both are merely provisional designations established by forceful naming within that which is beyond names and marks.
Names are established according to circumstances;
now, to demonstrate the profound and vast nature of this treatise,
I shall briefly set forth its various meanings.
Furthermore, since this treatise provides a comprehensive explanation of the Mahāyāna teachings, there is no meaning it does not encompass; thus, it contains all things.
Question: On what textual basis does the Preface author make this statement?
The answer concludes by stating:
"The profound meaning in its greatest part is what is called emptiness;
it is precisely the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa)."
To penetrate this meaning and be fully endowed with the six pāramitās without any obstruction is what is called the "site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa).
This constitutes the second section, which explains the three characters of the title; these three characters are precisely the [three] aspects.
The twelve are a major number for one direction; they treat illnesses and penetrate the channels.
"Branches" (zhi) refers to the distinct divisions, meaning the twelve differences.
This is one category of method.
There are further meanings already set forth in the commentaries.
A "gate" (mù) is a designation for unimpeded opening and penetration;
it relies upon the twelvefold verbal teachings to open up the wondrous principle of the true mark (dharmatā).
This is the contemplation of the mind by those who traverse the path.
As for the other meanings, they have already been set forth in the commentaries;
those who discuss them are explaining the treatise.
To exhaust its source is to exhaust the source of the three vehicles.
The source is but one;
in the past, it was expediently taught as three.
However, those who distinguish between them have not yet traced back to the root; thus they claim there are three.
If one examines and exhaustively investigates this, there is but a single source.
Therefore, the *Anantamukha-sūtra* says:
From a single dharma, immeasurable meanings arise.
That single dharma is precisely the signless (*animitta*).
Thus, this signlessness that is not a sign is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
The Lotus Sūtra says:
"Within the single Buddha-vehicle, one distinguishes and teaches three.
The Nirvāṇa Sūtra says:
This is a medicine of a single flavor that, according to where it flows, possesses six kinds of flavors, and even the flavors of the three vehicles;
all of these clarify the single source.
One who exhausts this principle causes those of the two vehicles above to change their course.
Now, let the six realms turn toward the fundamental source.
Since this treatise provides the correct exposition of the One Vehicle,
it shall cause sentient beings of the nine paths to equally attain Buddhahood.
Question: Why is it said that "breaking the three" reaches the source, while "washing away the six" exhausts the principle?
Answer: Although the names of these principles differ, their substance is one.
From a single source there arise three streams.
Because the various sons of the three vehicles have not exhausted their inquiry into that source, they speak of three differences.
If one seeks the source by following the streams, one will know that the source is but one.
Thus, one abandons the flow [of saṃsāra] to return to the source.
Since the six realms have already lost their way,
they constitute a departure from the principle of reality.
Therefore, it is necessary to clarify the ultimate principle.
Furthermore, by exhausting its source, one dispels the delusions of the sages;
by perfecting that principle, one shatters the confusion of ordinary beings.
This immediately causes one to realize that which is neither ordinary nor sagely, neither birth-and-death nor nirvana,
and so forth. Furthermore, it exhausts the source to repudiate internal delusion and exhausts the principle to shatter external attachments.
The various masters of doctrinal debate have not yet sought its source, and thus there are five hundred different schools;
yet one who exhausts the origin knows that the principle is but one.
Among the ninety-six heterodox paths, each claims to have attained the truth.
Therefore, heterodox paths are in great confusion;
if one were to exhaustively investigate the principle, these manifold differences would cease.
Furthermore, by tracing them to their source, one refutes the Mahāyāna practitioners who hold the attachment to "having something attained."
Those who have exhausted the principle are those who reject the study of the Hīnayāna.
It is only because they have not yet exhausted the principle that there is a "small" [vehicle].
If one were to exhaust the principle as it truly is, the principle would be non-dual.
How could there be distinctions of great or small?
However, it was spoken of as "one" merely because it was contrasted with different streams [of thought].

If one discards the differences while retaining the "one," or even extends this up to five hundred [teachings], all such views fail to exhaust the source and fail to fully realize the underlying principle.
One should deeply illuminate this meaning in order to perceive the intent of the person who composed the preface.
If there were even a single principle that was not fully exhausted, [the text] would have been incomplete; thus, the first two lines set forth two gates, which are now explained together.
Because they do not exhaust the principle, there are the six realms;
this refers to the divergence of delusion and the Way.
"Delusion" means being lost, and "the Way" means the principle.
This means that because one is deluded regarding the single Way, the six realms are formed.
If the single source is inexhaustible, then the many paths will flourish and spread.
"Many" (zhòng) refers to multiplicity; "paths" (tú) refers to ways (dào).
Because the ultimate source was not fully exhausted, there arose the divergent paths of the Three Vehicles and even the five hundred schools.
"Furshu" (扶疎) merely signifies the meaning of opening wide, expanding, and flourishing.
As for the traces of these distinct outcomes:
"Extraordinary" (*shu*) means "different.
It refers to the ultimate principle.
"Traces" (*ji*) refers to footprints.
Since it is the very footprint of the three vehicles and yet not extinguished in quiescence, how could one still attain Buddhahood?
Question: For what reason is this commentary composed?
Answer: If one were to provide a direct explanation, one should say that "discourse" (lun) refers to intersecting speech.
However, Master Rui now explains the three characters through three meanings.
As for the explanation of the twelve [categories], he explains them by taking the general significance of their numerical value.
This means that these twelve [factors] are not eliminated without being ill, not manifested without being taught,
not advanced without being reasoned, and not aroused without being contemplated;
thus, the number for each category is complete.
Therefore, it is said that there are twelve [categories].
Next, regarding the explanation of the title of the *Śāstra*, I shall explain it according to its characters.
Now, in explaining this *Śāstra*, I shall interpret it by taking the intent of the treatise and the functional efficacy of the treatise as my basis.
This is not an explanation by means of etymological definition. How is this known?
The text says:
The commentator seeks to exhaust its source and fully realize its principles;
thus, it is known that the explanation proceeds from the underlying intent and functional capacity.
That the diverse outcomes are not leveled is the third section, which sets forth the general purport of composing this treatise.
Furthermore, it is divided into three distinct sections:
first, an explanation of the causes and conditions for composing the treatise;
second, the actual exposition of the treatise.
Regarding the benefits of composing this treatise:
when the Great Being first established his great vow, he intended for all sentient beings of the nine paths to return to the single ultimate.
Yet now, they instead cling to the three vehicles and remain bound by their attachments to the six paths.
Is this not a cause for concern?
Therefore, when the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna opened up the path for those who have emerged,
the former was the compassionate mind, while the latter is the compassionate deed.
Furthermore, while the aforementioned [state] is the internal suffusion of great compassion,
the present [action] is the external rescue through skillful means;
thus, he utters words and composes this treatise.
There are two parts:
first, a general announcement of the twelve [sections];
second, the actual statement of composing the treatise.
The present [stage] is precisely the first.

"Emergence" (chu) means causing those in the six realms to emerge from the *pariccheda* (segmented) suffering, and enabling those of the three vehicles to depart from the *pariṇāma* (transformative) suffering;
because they are all equally exhorted to escape being burned by the two kinds of fires within the burning house, it is called "emergence."
Emergence must necessarily have a cause;
therefore, the twelve gates are established as the pathways for those who emerge,
so that they may emerge by means of these paths.
Regarding the establishment of twelve gates to rectify [this]:
previously, the general path was indicated; now, the specific matters of that path are described.
Beings of the six realms and those of the three vehicles have all alike lost the Way.
Therefore, it is weighed against error.
To sweep away that delusion and confusion, twelve [categories] are established to rectify it;
the Three Vehicles and the Six Paths are all deviant paths.
Now, these twelve gates are the correct path.
Question: How does one cause those in the six realms of existence to turn toward the fundamental source?
Answer: There are three kinds of ultimate emptiness.
As stated in the *Śata-śāstra*:
first, because the six realms of existence are originally quiescent,
they ultimately do not exist as six.
Second, because they are false and illusory, there are no six, namely the six realms;
nor are there six destinies.
It is like a thirsty person who sees water flowing within the six internal sense bases of a mirage.
In reality, there are no six destinies.
Thirdly, although the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas speak of six in accordance with the six [perceptions], there are likewise no six destinies.
It is like speaking of six waters in accordance with those who perceive water.
In reality, there are no six [realms],
for by awakening to the fact that the six are fundamentally unarisen, one turns the course of the six destinies back to their source.
Those of the Three Vehicles who shift their tracks [do so by this means].
The practitioners of the Two Vehicles have analyzed phenomena but have not yet realized their fundamental emptiness.
Although the Mahāsattvas know that phenomena are fundamentally empty, their illumination is still not exhaustive.
This treatise now reveals ultimate emptiness, the sphere of practice of all Buddhas.
This is because it causes those of the three vehicles to ultimately and thoroughly comprehend [reality].
Within each and every gate, all are designated as "ultimate emptiness" (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
This is because ultimate emptiness is the sphere of practice for all Buddhas. Question: What is meant by "opening the path" and "blocking the path"?
Answer: There are two kinds of blockages:
first, the long-standing delusions of the six realms of existence.
Second is attachment to the teachings of the two vehicles.
Now, by removing these two obstructions, one opens up the twelve paths;
from each and every path, one enters into the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
To rectify this by means of twelve principles, both existence and non-existence are fully elucidated, and no matter is left unexhausted.
Second, the explicit clarification of the composition of this treatise consists of five transitions and ten negations.
That is to say: neither internal nor external;
neither phenomena nor persons;
neither conditioned by objects nor observing them.
Neither false nor true;
neither gained nor lost.
Its words are skillful and its meaning profound.
Its phrasing is concise while its principles are profound.
There is no flaw it does not rectify and no teaching it does not expound.
There is no principle it does not penetrate and no condition it does not benefit.
Now, first, we shall refute internal illness.
Illnesses are manifold, yet they are rooted in both being and non-being;
furthermore, they are the very foundation that obstructs the Middle Way.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata always teaches the Dharma by relying on the two truths.
Because [sentient beings] do not comprehend the two truths of existence and non-existence regarding causes and conditions,
they fall into the two maladies of inherent existence and inherent non-existence.
Since there is no teaching that does not encompass the two truths,
there is likewise no delusion regarding the two truths that is not subsumed [by them].
Furthermore, the followers of the Hīnayāna are mostly afflicted by the disease of clinging to existence.
Those who study the Great Vehicle often stagnate in non-sickness;
furthermore, ordinary beings are attached to existence while those of the Two Vehicles stagnate in emptiness.
Moreover, those with much craving are attached to existence, while those with many views are attached to emptiness.
Therefore, this treatise refutes these two [extremes].
Question: Does it merely refute existence and non-existence, or does it also establish existence and non-existence?
Answer: It possesses both meanings.
One must first refute existence and non-existence before one can then establish existence and non-existence;
thus, the passage below stating that "there are two truths" refers precisely to this matter.
It is further said:
"To merely explain emptiness is to set forth the primary meaning (paramārtha).
To thoroughly penetrate emptiness is to penetrate the Mahāyāna."
To be fully endowed with the six perfections refers to the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Question: What is meant by "comprehensive elucidation"?
Answer: There are three kinds of meanings.
First, it is called "comprehensive" because it first refutes existence and subsequently refutes non-existence.
Second, it is called "comprehensive" because it presents the conventional truth and further presents the ultimate truth.
Third, there is no ailment that is not cured and no teaching that is not fully articulated; thus, the intention of the Great Being is completely expressed.
Therefore, it is said that they are "comprehensive.
"Thoroughness" (*chàng*) also has three aspects:
first, the removal of illness through the presence [of medicine] is thoroughness.
Second, the teaching of the two truths is universally employed for the purpose of thorough elucidation;
third, the thorough elucidation consists in fully expressing the minds of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
When all phenomena are exhausted within existence and non-existence, one finds no further agency in the creative forces of transformation.
Above, the internal delusions were refuted; now, the external attachments are being repudiated.
This treatise primarily refutes the internal [view];
therefore, it first repudiates the internal while incidentally refuting the external.
Therefore, the latter is excluded.
Regarding the "Creator," Zhuang Zhou said:
"The *wangliang* [demon] arises because of a shadow."
The shadow arises from the form;
the form is caused by the process of transformation (zhao-hua).
Yet, as for this process of transformation, one knows not its cause.
Now, by temporarily casting out Zhuang Zhou of Zhendan, one may shatter the heterodoxies of India;
this is truly because there are no distinct heterodox schools in this land,
and within a single statement, both perspectives are simultaneously exhausted.
Therefore, this [text] rejects the one and rebukes the other.
Question: At what point in this treatise is the theory of creation refuted?
Answer: It is refuted under the section on the "Creator" regarding Maheśvara.
This refers precisely to that matter.
Because Īśvara is able to create all transformations, he is called the "Creator.
Question: For what reason is Īśvara refuted?
Answer: Existence and non-existence are the root of internal delusion;
the process of creation is the foundation of external attachment.
Therefore, by cutting down its root, the branches and twigs will naturally wither away.
Question: For what reason do you say that when existence and non-existence are exhausted, the creative power of transformation (*zaohua*) ceases?
Answer: By refuting existence and non-existence, not only are internal afflictions eliminated, but external transformation is also destroyed.
As for saying its creative power has ceased, it is because deluded people cling to the notion that Maheśvara creates all transformations, and thus regard this as a great achievement.
By causing them to be shattered and destroyed, one realizes that the autonomous self cannot create;
hence it is said that [the self] perishes.
Principle culminates in emptiness, clarifying that dharmas are without self.
Regarding "losing the self at the two limits":
this means destroying the notion of a person so that one may attain the selflessness of persons.
Previously, the two dharmas of internal and external were eliminated; now, the two types of persons—internal and external—are successively refuted.
This gives rise to the two emptinesses of persons and phenomena.
As for why phenomena are refuted first and persons afterwards, that is the position of the treatise itself.
Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "Because conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are empty."
How much more so in my case?
Furthermore, while the preceding sections mostly employed reductio ad absurdum (*prasanga*),
it is only upon reaching the section on the "agent" that the person [the self] is formally refuted.
The reason why the Dharma is mentioned first and persons later is that the Dharma is fundamental while persons are derivative;
the Dharma is difficult [to understand] while persons are easy.
The Dharma is internal and persons are external.
Non-Buddhists reckon that persons are internal and mostly cling to dharmas as being external;
thus, [this teaching] directly refutes the internal and indirectly refutes the external.
Furthermore, if one follows the sequence of the gates of contemplation, one first clarifies the emptiness of persons and subsequently distinguishes the emptiness of phenomena;
however, this is now according to the gate of exposition.
Moreover, it is because those of the Lesser Vehicle already know there is no person yet still cling to the existence of phenomena.
One cannot turn from the Small Vehicle into the Great Vehicle.
Now, because I wish to cause them to turn from the Small Vehicle into the Great Vehicle,
I first refute the Dharma and subsequently eliminate the person.
The "empty position" is the true mark (lakṣaṇa);
it is another name for the dharma-position of suchness (tathatā).
This is now clarified.
Conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are ultimately empty.
The ultimate limit of principle resides in this emptiness;
therefore, it is said that "the limit of principle is a position of vacuity."
Because both the self of the internal [Buddhist] schools and the external [non-Buddhist] schools are eliminated, one loses the notion of a self at both extremes.
Furthermore, since the preceding refutation of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena has shown them to be empty,
the conditioned self and the unconditioned self are likewise empty.
Therefore, it is said that one loses the self at the two limits.
Furthermore, both being attached to the aggregates and being detached from the aggregates constitute the two limits.
Moreover, the self and what belongs to the self are also called the two limits.
The third section, "Losing Myself in the Abandonment of the Fish-trap," states:
Although the preceding [section] removed both the internal and external, and simultaneously refuted both person and phenomena,
it has not yet refuted the very act of refutation and establishment itself.
However, although the contemplation of conditions has been exhausted, the conditions themselves have not yet been fully contemplated.
Now, wishing to shatter both the provisional and the established, so that both conditions and contemplation are simultaneously quiescent,
this pair [of contemplations] is presented.
Question: Master Rui, what textual passages did you rely upon to form this interpretation?
Answer: The "Gate of the Three Subsequent Periods" (hōsanjimon) explicitly clarifies the refutation of refutations;
prior to that, it clarifies the removal of established positions.
Therefore, I have set forth this meaning.
"Dropping the trap" (*luo quan*) is another name for "dropping" as "removing and extinguishing.
Thus, it is also called "extinguishing the trap" (*wang quan*), "removing the trap" (*chu quan*), and so forth.
Now, if one wishes to eliminate the "self" that is to be refuted,
one must necessarily discard the "means of refutation.
If the means of refutation is not discarded, then that which is to be refuted will not be exhausted.
Therefore it is said: "The loss of the self lies in the dropping of the trap.
A net is used for catching fish;
a snare is used for catching animals.
Question: For what reason is the "ability to refute" (nigrahasthāna) considered a "fishing net" (śuān)?

Answer: The reason the Master of the Treatise composed the teachings on the "twelve gates of the ability to refute" was solely because he wished to cure the ailments of sentient beings, such as the notions of a self (ātman) and a person (pudgala).
Therefore, the teaching of refutation is treated as a trap;
just as one does not need the trap once the fish is caught,
when the illness has been cured, the teaching is discarded.
When the trap is discarded, what remains is that which was entrusted to it.
This explains the reason why the capacity for refutation can be forgotten;
thus, the trap of refutation is thereby eliminated.
One must necessarily discard that which was used as a vessel;
once the "trap" (suan) that served as the vessel for the refutation has fulfilled its purpose and the "disease" that was to be refuted has been eliminated,
how could one possibly retain the vessel?
One must forget this "ability to lodge" and that which is "shattered" before one can attain purity;
"forgetting" (wei) is simply another name for "forgetting.
This employs Zhuang Zhou’s essential point regarding the ultimate convergence of things, expressed in his words about "forgetting what is lodged."
"When both the trap and the fish are forgotten, one may for the first time approach the reality;
when both refutation and establishment are forgotten and both the conditions and the contemplation are stilled,
one may for the first time draw near to the true mark of all phenomena."
"Ke ji" (可幾) means "near.
When "almost" (ji hu) reaches the state of reality, then the fourth pair—where both the real and the unreal are darkly merged—is realized.
This intention eliminates the duality of the negator and the negated.
Now, furthermore, this is the dissolution of both the "refuter" and the "refuted" as real entities.
"The boundlessness of gain and loss" is the fifth pair.
